script_old: Peter Pan's copyright expired in the U.K., and a children's hospital can still collect royalties. In nineteen twenty-nine, J.M. Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to Great Ormond Street Hospital, a children's hospital in London. Normally, when a copyright expires, the work enters the public domain, and anyone can use it without paying. In the U.K., the copyright in Peter Pan expired at the end of nineteen eighty-seven. But Parliament did something unusual. In the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act of nineteen eighty-eight, section three hundred one gives the hospital's trustees a right to a royalty for public performance, commercial publication, or communication to the public of the play, or any adaptation of it, even though the copyright had expired. So the copyright clock stopped, but a separate royalty stream kept flowing to the hospital. The hospital says all U.K. performances of Peter Pan support its charity, including theatre, school and pantomime productions. And it has never disclosed how much Peter Pan has raised, in keeping with Barrie's wishes. Here's the limit. This is a special royalty right created by U.K. law.
